summary: Describes how a certification authority in the RPKI does a planned change of its key pair, and what it means for relying parties that keep a local cache of the repository. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This document says how a certificate authority in the RPKI changes its key. The change is done in stages, with a waiting period, so that nobody checking the certificates is ever left unable to verify them.

questions: how to roll over an rpki key
how long is the rpki staging period
how does a ca roll over its key
what must relying parties do during key rollover
subtitle: How an RPKI certificate authority replaces its key without breaking the people checking its certificates.

tldr.problem: A certificate authority in the RPKI cannot simply swap its key, because relying parties cache the objects it publishes and a careless change could make them reject valid attestations.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a six-step procedure in which the authority creates a new instance with a new key, publishes it, waits out a staging period of at least 24 hours, then republishes everything under the new key and revokes the old certificate.
tldr.outcome: It is Best Current Practice 174 from February 2012, and it keeps relying parties able to validate every authentic object in the RPKI throughout the change.

facts.label: Manifest end-entity certificate
facts.value: Single use, private key destroyed after signing

today: RFC 6489 is Best Current Practice 174, published in February 2012. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the procedure RPKI certificate authorities follow when they replace their keys.

sections.title: What a Key Rollover Is
sections.content:
The document describes an algorithm for a Certification Authority (CA) in the Resource Public Key Infrastructure to roll over its key pair. The procedure is deliberately conservative: the CA's actions are not intended to disrupt the normal operation of relying parties, which keep a local cached copy of the RPKI distributed repository. Following it, relying parties stay in a position to validate all authentic objects in the RPKI using the validation procedure of RFC 6480 at all times.

A CA in the RPKI issues CA certificates, end-entity certificates and CRLs, and a CA instance is associated with a single key pair. So a CA does not really roll over a key. It creates a new instance of itself with a new key pair and substitutes that new instance into the RPKI hierarchy in place of the old one. Over time a CA that rolls over regularly will have many instances.

The focus is on planned rollover, not on an emergency rollover after a suspected or detected private key compromise, although the same procedure applies in an emergency apart from the duration of the staging period. The critical requirement is that the rollover must not create a moment in which a relying party is led to a wrong conclusion about the authenticity of an RPKI attestation. A CA cannot assume that every relying party does path validation and path discovery in the same way, so the procedure MUST preserve the integrity of the CRL Distribution Points, Subject Information Access and Authority Information Access pointers in RPKI certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the key is not a one-line change, because other people hold cached copies of everything the authority has published. The procedure is designed so nobody is ever left holding something they cannot check.

sections.title: The Three CA States
sections.content:
The procedure describes three CA states. The CURRENT CA is the active instance that accepts and processes certificate issuance and revocation requests. The algorithm starts here, with the key of the CURRENT CA being the one to be rolled over.

The NEW CA is the instance being created. It is not active, so it accepts and processes neither issuance nor revocation requests. It SHOULD issue a CRL and an end-entity certificate in association with its manifest, so that it is a trivial, complete and consistent instance of a CA.

The OLD CA is the instance in the process of being removed. It cannot process any issuance or revocation request. It will continue to issue regularly scheduled CRLs and an end-entity certificate as part of updating its manifest to reflect the updated CRL, so that the objects pointing at it remain valid until its certificate is revoked.

While the CURRENT and NEW instances share a single repository publication point, each CA has its own CRL and its own manifest. The NEW CA initially publishes an empty CRL and a manifest with a single entry for that CRL, while the CURRENT CA keeps its own published CRL and manifest at the same publication point.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three roles during the change: the authority you are using now, the new one being prepared, and the old one on its way out. The outgoing authority keeps publishing its revocation list until it is cancelled.

sections.title: The Rollover Steps
sections.content:
The steps must be performed in the order given, and the process MUST be run through to completion. Unless stated otherwise, each step SHOULD be performed without any intervening delay.

The first step is to generate a new key pair for the NEW CA, which MUST differ from the pair in use by the CURRENT CA. The second step is to generate a certificate request with that key pair and pass it to the CA that issued the CURRENT CA certificate. The request MUST include the same SIA extension that is present in the CURRENT CA certificate, and the resulting NEW CA certificate will carry a subject name chosen by the issuer that MUST be distinct from the one in the CURRENT CA certificate.

The third step is to publish the NEW CA's CRL and manifest. That means waiting for the issuer to publish the NEW CA certificate, then using the new key to generate an initially empty CRL and publishing it at the NEW CA's publication point, with a nextUpdate value that will cause it to be replaced at the end of the staging period. Then a fresh key pair is generated and an end-entity certificate request is made with an AIA value pointing at the NEW CA's repository publication point. The single-use certificate that comes back is the manifest end-entity certificate. A manifest containing the new CA's CRL as its only entry is signed with that key and published, and the private key associated with the manifest end-entity certificate is then destroyed.

The fourth step is the staging period. Its duration is chosen by the CA but SHOULD be no less than 24 hours, and it exists so that all relying parties can download the NEW CA certificate before any certificate, CRL or signed object is published under it. During this period the NEW CA SHOULD reissue, but not publish, everything issued under the CURRENT CA. The CURRENT CA SHOULD keep accepting and processing certificate issuance requests and MUST keep accepting and processing revocation requests. Anything issued by the CURRENT CA during the staging period MUST be reissued under the NEW CA, and anything revoked under the CURRENT CA MUST NOT be reissued.

The fifth step happens when the staging period ends. The NEW CA MUST publish the products it has reissued, replacing the corresponding products of the CURRENT CA at the same publication point, and its manifest now lists all of them. At that point the CURRENT CA becomes the OLD CA and the NEW CA becomes the CURRENT CA, and the OLD CA issues a manifest listing only its own CRL. That step is expected to be very brief, perhaps a few minutes, but it is desirable that relying parties see it as atomic.

The sixth step is to request revocation of the OLD CA certificate and submit that request to the certificate's issuer. When the OLD CA certificate is revoked, its CRL and its manifest are removed from the repository and the private key for the OLD CA is destroyed.
sections.plainLanguage: Six steps: make a new key, get a certificate for it, publish an empty list of revocations under the new key, wait at least a day, then swap everything over at once and finally cancel the old certificate.

sections.title: What Relying Parties Must Do
sections.content:
The procedure defines a staging period of no shorter than 24 hours, and that period exists so that relying parties have time to fetch the new CA certificate before anything is published under it. Relying parties who maintain a local cache of the distributed RPKI repository MUST perform a local cache synchronization operation against the repository at regular intervals of no longer than 24 hours. In other words, if a checker only refreshes its copy once a day, the staging period is long enough for it to pick up the new certificate in time.

The document makes no demand beyond that. Because the staging period imposes no additional burden on relying parties, there is no stipulated or recommended maximum length for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone keeping a cached copy of the repository has to refresh it at least once a day. That is the only thing the change asks of them.

sections.title: Reissuing Certificates and Signed Objects
sections.content:
These rules apply when a CA reissues subordinate certificates and RPKI signed objects as part of the rollover. CRLs and manifests are not reissued in this sense, because they are generated for each CA instance: a manifest catalogues the contents of a publication point relative to a CA instance, and a CRL lists revoked certificates relative to a CA instance.

When a CA reissues a CA certificate it copies all of the field and extension values from the old certificate into the new one. The only exceptions are that the notBefore value MAY be set to the current date and time and the serial number MAY change. Because the reissued certificate is issued by a different CA instance, the serial number is not required to change, but the CA MUST ensure that each certificate issued under a specific CA instance carries a unique serial number.

An RPKI signed object is a Cryptographic Message Syntax signed-data object containing an end-entity certificate and a payload. When a key rollover occurs, that end-entity certificate MUST be reissued under the key of the NEW CA. A CA MAY copy all fields and extensions across and change only the notBefore date and the serial number, in which case the new certificate goes into the CMS wrapper and the signed context stays the same. Alternatively the CA MAY generate a new key pair for that end-entity certificate, in which case the object content MUST be resigned under the matching private key. The end-entity certificate then MUST contain a new public key and a new notBefore value, MAY contain a new notAfter value, and otherwise keeps all other field and extension values unchanged apart from those relating to the digital signature and its certificate validation path. The presence or absence of the signing-time and binary-signing-time attributes MUST NOT affect the validity of the signed object.
sections.plainLanguage: When the authority reissues a certificate as part of the change, it keeps everything the same except the dates and the serial number, so that the pointers inside the certificates still point at the right places.

sections.title: How Often a Key Should Change
sections.content:
No key should be used forever. The longer a key is in use, the greater the probability that it has been compromised through carelessness, accident, espionage or cryptanalysis. Infrequent key rollover increases the risk that the rollover procedure will not be followed to the appropriate level of precision, which raises the risk of an operational failure of some form during the rollover.

Regular scheduling of key rollover is generally considered part of prudent key management, but rollover does impose additional operational burdens on both the CA and the population of relying parties. A CA should therefore balance security and operational impact when choosing key lifetimes. The intervals should be frequent enough to minimise the risks of key compromise and to keep local operational proficiency with the rollover process, but key lifetimes should be sufficiently long that the load of rollover events across the whole RPKI does not place an excessive burden on relying parties. Relying parties are encouraged to maintain an accurate local cache of the current state of the RPKI, which implies frequent queries to the repository to detect changes. When a CA rekeys it changes many signed objects, and that affects every relying party.
sections.plainLanguage: Keys should not live forever, but changing them often makes everybody's job harder, because each change touches every object the authority has signed. The document leaves the balance to each authority.

viz.caption: THE THREE STATES OF A CA DURING A ROLLOVER
THE SIX STEPS OF THE ROLLOVER PROCEDURE

cells: Generate a new key pair for the NEW CA, different from the CURRENT one
Request a NEW CA certificate from the issuer, with the same SIA extension
Publish an empty CRL and a one-entry manifest under the NEW CA
Wait out the staging period, at least 24 hours, reissuing products but not publishing them
Publish the reissued products, then the NEW CA becomes CURRENT and the old one becomes OLD
Revoke the OLD CA certificate, remove its CRL and manifest, destroy its private key
